The 2025–26 Premier Play season is the thirty-first Pro Tour season for Magic: The Gathering. The season opens with Regional Championships in October 2025 and ends with the 2026 World Championship in November, 2026.[1]

Regional Championships 10

The Regional Championships between October 11 to November 23, 2025 awarded invites to Pro Tour Lorwyn Eclipsed and the 2026 World Championship. The format was Modern Constructed.[2] For South America and Brazil, Devir BR assumed the Regional Championship partnerships from Magicsur and City Class Games respectively.[3] Going forward, there will be one Regional Championship event covering the combined Brazil and South America regions, with a total $40,000 prize pool, ten Pro Tour invitations, and two World Championship invitations per each event.

Arena Championship 10

Arena Championship 10 took place on December 20–21, 2025.[4] The format was Timeless Constructed. 112 players participated in the tournament, the largest for an Arena Championship since the series began.[5] Many high-profile players qualified, such as World Champions Nathan Steuer and Jun'ya Iyanaga and Pro Tour Champions Ondřej Stráský, Michael DeBenedetto-Plummer, Matt Nass and Arne Huschenbeth.

Timeless was a uniquely unexplored format for a high-level tournament, given the number of power level outliers and little resemblance to its closest analogue of Vintage. Strip Mine was legal at four copies, the only format in which this has been true in nearly three decades. The most played deck was a superpowered version of the Modern Boros Energy deck, here a Mardu build with Lurrus of the Dream-Den as a Companion, another card banned out of many formats. Vintage-restricted Necropotence and its descendant Necrodominance powered by Dark Ritual was second-most popular, backed with Entomb-Reanimate. Legacy staples of Mono-Red Prison and Dimir Reanimator have their cores intact, rounding out the top four archetypes.[6]

Pro Tour Lorwyn Eclipsed

The first Pro Tour of 2026 took place on January 30 – February 1, 2026, at Richmond, Virginia, USA. This Pro Tour was not held at a MagicCon; it was a closed event for participants and was not open to the public.[10] The format was Lorwyn Eclipsed Booster Draft and Standard Constructed.

Arena Championship 11

Arena Championship 11 took place on February 21–22, 2026. The format was Standard Constructed.[11] 120 players were eligible to participate in the tournament, another slight uptick from the previous event. The field was headlined by Hall of Famers Seth Manfield and Shota Yasooka alongside Pro Tour champions Christoffer Larsen, Arne Huschenbeth, Autumn Burchett, and Kyle Rose.

Standard proved to be a broad and diverse format, but the field for this tournament coalesced into three prior-known frontrunners of Mono-Green Landfall at 26 pilots, Izzet Lessons at 21 pilots and Simic Rhythm at 14 pilots, totaling to roughly half the field. Notably, the many Cub deck variants of the Pro Tour were largely winnowed to that of Landfall and Rhythm, while the World Champion's deck Lessons still stood strong after the metagame shifted.

Arena Championship 12

Arena Championship 12 took place on May 23–24, 2026. The format was Historic Constructed.[11] 110 players qualified for the event, Champions amongst them Arne Huschenbeth, Christoffer Larsen, Wyatt Darby, Elias Watsfeldt, Ondřej Stráský and returning veterans Farid Meraghni and Daniel Zink, the latter having not played in an event for two decades.

Historic had not been seen for multiple cycles; the last was Arena Championship 6, where the dominant Horizons Energy decks were nerfed with the August rebalancing of that year. The most common decks were a collection from across formats: an upgraded version of competitor Zevin Faust's personally developed Standard Azorius Prison deck, a variant of the Modern Esper Blink decks like from Pro Tour Edge of Eternities, and the perennially viable Izzet Phoenix decks. In fourth place was the first Historic-exclusive deck of Jund Goyfs, using the Modern Horizons 3 pair of Pyrogoyf and Barrowgoyf that are Legacy-legal but are too slow for that format. Notable was also the influence of digital cards Juggernaut Peddler and Fragment Reality, interactive spells that have digital-only downsides that are often negated by the nature of the format.
